segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After this the Lord appointed seventy-two others as well and sent them out two by two ahead of him into every town and place where he himself was about to go.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few. So ask the Lord of the harvest to send out workers into his harvest.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Go! Look, I am sending you out like lambs among wolves.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Do not carry a purse or a bag or sandals, and greet no one along the road.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Whatever house you enter, first say, ‘Peace to this house.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest on him; but if not, it will return to you.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Stay in that same house, eating and drinking what they provide, for the worker deserves his wages. Do not move around from house to house.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And whatever town you enter where they welcome you, eat what is set before you,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: heal the sick who are in it, and say to them, ‘The kingdom of God has come near to you.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But whatever town you enter where they do not welcome you, go out into its streets and say,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: ‘Even the dust of your town that clings to our feet we wipe off against you. Yet know this: the kingdom of God has come near.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I tell you, it will be more bearable on that day for Sodom than for that town.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the deeds of power done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have turned back long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But it will be more bearable for Tyre and Sidon at the judgment than for you.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And you, Capernaum, will you be lifted up to heaven? You will be brought down to Hades.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Whoever listens to you listens to me, and whoever rejects you rejects me; and whoever rejects me rejects the one who sent me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The seventy-two returned with joy, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, even the demons submit to us in your name!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I was watching Satan fall like lightning from heaven.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Look, I have given you the authority to tread on snakes and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing will harm you at all.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Yet do not rejoice in this, that the spirits submit to you, but rejoice that your names have been written in the heavens.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At that very hour he exulted in the Holy Spirit and said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I praise you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and intelligent and revealed them to infants. Yes, Father, for this was your good pleasure.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: All things have been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows who the Son is except the Father, or who the Father is except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then turning to the disciples, he said privately,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see!

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For I tell you that many prophets and kings wanted to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Just then an expert in the law stood up to put him to the test, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “What is written in the Law? How do you read it?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength and with all your mind, and your neighbor as yourself.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “You have answered correctly. Do this, and you will live.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he, wanting to justify himself, said to Jesus,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “And who is my neighbor?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus took up the question and said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among bandits, who stripped him, beat him, and went away, leaving him half dead.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Now by chance a priest was going down that road, and when he saw him he passed by on the other side.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: In the same way a Levite also, when he came to the place and saw him, passed by on the other side.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But a Samaritan who was traveling came to where he was, and when he saw him he was moved with compassion.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: He went to him and bandaged his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. Then he put him on his own animal, brought him to an inn, and took care of him.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The next day he took out two denarii, gave them to the innkeeper, and said, ‘Take care of him, and whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I come back.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Which of these three do you think became a neighbor to the man who fell among the bandits?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “The one who showed him mercy.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Go, and you do the same.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As they went on their way, he entered a village, and a woman named Martha welcomed him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She had a sister called Mary, who sat down at the feet of Jesus and was listening to his word.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Martha was distracted by all the serving. She came up and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to do the serving alone? So tell her to help me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the Lord answered her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: but few things are needed—or only one. For Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her.”

notes.note: The manuscripts are closely divided between “seventy-two” and “seventy,” here and in verse 17, and both readings are early. The Greek text followed here prints “seventy-two”; many English versions read “seventy.” Either number may echo a traditional count of the world’s nations, but that connection is uncertain.

“Son of” is a Semitic idiom for someone characterized by or belonging to a thing, so “a son of peace” is a person disposed to peace and ready to receive the greeting. Some translations paraphrase it as “a peaceful person” or “someone who promotes peace.” The idiom is kept here because the Greek keeps it.

The Greek is the ordinary word for “power,” used in the plural for acts that display it. The same word appears as “power” in verse 19, and this rendering keeps that link visible. There is no dispute about the meaning, and “miracles” is an equally acceptable translation.

Most translations have “repented,” which in modern English centers on feeling sorry. The Greek word carries the prophets’ call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct, and sackcloth and ashes were the outward signs of it. “Repent” remains the standard rendering and is understood by many readers to include a change of life.

The Greek is plural here, a Semitic turn of phrase for God’s dwelling, while verses 15, 18 and 21 use the singular. Most translations flatten the plural to “heaven.” The image is of a heavenly register in which the names of God’s people are recorded.

Many translations have “lawyer,” which now suggests an attorney who represents clients in court. The word names a man learned in the Law of Moses and its interpretation, a group overlapping with those the Gospels call scribes. Several modern versions also use “expert in the law.”

The adjective comes from the word for “age,” and in Jewish usage “eternal life” is the life of the age to come, a matter of kind as well as length. The man is asking how to have a share in that coming age. “Eternal” is the standard rendering and is kept here.

Greek distinguishes this word from the one for a thief who steals by stealth; it denotes armed, violent men who plunder travelers, often in gangs. Most translations have “robbers,” which is not wrong but can suggest a burglar or mugger. The steep desert road from Jerusalem down to Jericho was known for such attacks.

Jews and Samaritans had a long history of religious and ethnic hostility, and each regarded the other’s worship as illegitimate. After a priest and a Levite, hearers would likely have expected an ordinary Israelite as the third traveler. Making a Samaritan the one who helps is the shock of the story.
A denarius was a Roman silver coin, roughly a day’s pay for a laborer. Two denarii would have covered a number of days’ board at an inn, though exactly how many is uncertain.

To sit at a teacher’s feet was the posture of a disciple receiving instruction; Paul uses the same expression of his training under Gamaliel in Acts 22:3. Mary is taking the place of a pupil, not merely sitting nearby. Some manuscripts read “the Lord’s feet” here.

notes.phrase: but few things are needed—or only one
notes.note: The manuscripts differ here. Many, followed by most English translations, read simply “but one thing is necessary”; others, including some early witnesses and the Greek text translated here, have the longer form “few things are needed, or one.” In the longer form “few things” may refer first to dishes for the meal before the saying narrows to the one thing that matters; which reading is original is disputed.

Frequent across the New Testament and split between “authority,” “power” and “right,” and it needs to stay distinct from δύναμις, which stands beside it in this verse.
Used of everything from Galilean villages to Jerusalem and Rome, so a rule for “town” versus “city” is needed to keep chapters consistent.
Means “praise” or “thank” in this Septuagintal sense but “confess” elsewhere, and translations vary between “praise” and “thank” in the parallel at Matthew 11:25.
Recurs in the Gospels, Paul and Hebrews with renderings ranging over “infants,” “babes,” “little children” and “the childlike,” which obscures a shared image.
